response.title: what should i buy to back up my home office internet and computer for a full day
response.answer:
To keep your home office computer and internet running for a full 24 hours during a power outage, I'd recommend a combination of:

Portable power station (LiFePO4 battery) — provides most of the energy for your computer, monitors, and networking equipment.

Small UPS (uninterruptible power supply) — keeps your computer and router running without interruption when the power goes out.

Backup internet connection (5G or cellular hotspot) — protects you if your cable or fiber internet goes down, even when your router still has power.

The most important purchase is the power station. A normal $100–$200 UPS typically lasts minutes, not an entire day.

How much battery capacity do you need?

Here are rough estimates for a 24-hour outage, assuming continuous use.

Home office setup

Laptop + router + modem

Laptop + monitor + internet

2.3–3.5 kWh




Desktop + monitor + internet

	

150–250 W

	

4.2–7 kWh




High-performance desktop + dual monitors

	

300–500 W

	

8–14 kWh

These estimates include some battery and inverter losses. Actual usage varies considerably, particularly for desktop PCs.

My default recommendation: If you're using a laptop with an external monitor, aim for a 3 kWh battery system. If you're using a desktop, measure its power consumption before buying.

The EcoFlow has a stated 10 ms transfer time, while the Anker F3000 specifies 20 ms. A dedicated UPS is preferable if your desktop cannot tolerate even a brief interruption. 
EcoFlow
+1

Don't forget internet redundancy

Battery power keeps your router running, but your ISP may still lose service.

For dependable work-from-home connectivity, I would also have a cellular backup, preferably on a different network from your primary internet provider. Your phone's hotspot can be a cost-effective starting point; a dedicated 5G router is better for automatic failover.
